title: Cells, and how they are specialised

tips.title: Eukaryotic means the DNA is boxed
tips.body: **Eukaryotic** cells keep their genetic material **inside a nucleus**. **Prokaryotic** cells do not — their DNA sits **free in the cytoplasm**. Animals and plants are eukaryotic; bacteria are prokaryotic. That one difference is the definition, and it is what a one-mark question wants.

tips.title: Plant cells have everything animal cells have
tips.body: A plant cell has the **four** animal parts — nucleus, cell membrane, mitochondria, ribosomes — **plus three more**: cell wall, chloroplasts and a permanent vacuole. So the question is never *which does a plant cell lack*, only which it **adds**.

tips.title: Name the part and its job
tips.body: A question about a sub-cellular structure almost always wants **both** the part and **what it does**. *Mitochondria* earns less than *mitochondria, the site of aerobic respiration, which releases energy*. The spec says the structures are to be related **to their functions**.

tips.title: Haploid in both gametes, for one reason
tips.body: The sperm nucleus and the egg nucleus are **both haploid** — one set of chromosomes each. That is so fertilisation restores the **diploid** number rather than doubling it each generation. Give the reason, not just the word.

tips.title: Cilia move mucus, they do not trap it
tips.body: The **goblet cells** make the mucus and the mucus traps the dust and bacteria. The **cilia** then **beat to sweep the mucus** up the airway to the throat. Saying cilia trap dirt describes the wrong cell.

steps.title: Eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells
steps.body:
**All living things are made of cells**, and cells come in two kinds.

- **Eukaryotic** cells keep their genetic material **enclosed in a nucleus**. Animal cells and plant cells are eukaryotic.
- **Prokaryotic** cells have **no nucleus**. Their genetic material sits **free in the cytoplasm**. **Bacteria** are prokaryotic.

**That is the whole distinction**, and it is worth being exact about, because it is a one-mark question that students often answer with size instead. Prokaryotic cells *are* much smaller — but small is a **consequence**, not the definition. A question asking *what makes a cell prokaryotic?* is answered by **no nucleus**.

**Some parts are in every cell**, whichever kind it is:

- a **cell membrane**, which controls what enters and leaves
- **ribosomes**, where **proteins are made**
- **genetic material**, whether boxed in a nucleus or loose

So the shared list is as useful as the difference. If you are asked what a bacterium and a human cheek cell have in common, those three are the answer.

steps.title: Animal and plant cells, part by part
steps.body:
**The spec asks you to relate each sub-cellular structure to its function**, so learn them in pairs — the part and the job.

**In an animal cell:**

- **Nucleus** — contains the **genetic material (DNA)**, which **controls the activities of the cell**
- **Cell membrane** — **controls what enters and leaves** the cell
- **Mitochondria** — the site of **aerobic respiration**, which **releases energy** for the cell
- **Ribosomes** — where **protein synthesis** happens

**A plant cell has all four of those, and three more:**

- **Cell wall**, made of **cellulose** — **strengthens** the cell and stops it bursting
- **Chloroplasts** — contain **chlorophyll** and are the site of **photosynthesis**
- **Permanent vacuole** — filled with **cell sap**, it keeps the cell **firm (turgid)**

**Notice the pattern.** The three extra parts are all about being a plant: making food from light, and standing up without a skeleton. A plant cell is an animal cell plus the equipment for those two jobs.

**A caution about chloroplasts.** Not every plant cell has them — **root cells do not**, because there is no light underground. So *all plant cells contain chloroplasts* is wrong, and root hair cells are the example that proves it.

steps.title: Bacterial cells
steps.body:
A bacterial cell is **prokaryotic**, and the spec names exactly **five** features:

- **Chromosomal DNA** — a **single loop** of DNA, free in the cytoplasm, carrying most of the genetic material
- **Plasmid DNA** — **small rings** of DNA carrying **extra genes**, such as resistance to an antibiotic
- **Cell membrane** — controls what enters and leaves
- **Ribosomes** — where proteins are made
- **Flagella** — long tails that **rotate to move the cell**

**The two kinds of DNA are the part worth understanding.** The chromosomal loop is the bacterium's main set of instructions. **Plasmids are extra, and they can be passed from one bacterium to another** — which is how **antibiotic resistance spreads** so quickly through a population. That link is why plasmids are on the specification at all, and it comes back when you meet antibiotic resistance.

**Flagella are for movement.** A question showing a bacterium with a long tail and asking what it is for wants **movement**, not gas exchange and not feeding.

**What a bacterium does not have:** no nucleus, no mitochondria, no chloroplasts. It still respires — the reactions happen in the cytoplasm and at the membrane instead.

steps.title: Sperm cells and egg cells
steps.body:
**A specialised cell has a structure that fits its job**, and the spec names the adaptations it wants.

**The sperm cell** has to reach the egg and get inside it:

- an **acrosome** at the front, containing **enzymes** that **digest through the egg's membrane**
- a **haploid nucleus** — **one set of chromosomes**
- **many mitochondria**, releasing the energy needed to **swim**
- a **tail**, which beats to **propel** the cell

**The egg cell** has to nourish the embryo and admit exactly one sperm:

- **nutrients in the cytoplasm**, to **feed the embryo** after fertilisation
- a **haploid nucleus** — one set of chromosomes
- the **cell membrane changes after fertilisation**, so **no more sperm can enter**

**Both gametes are haploid, and there is one reason.** Each carries **half** the chromosomes, so when they fuse the **diploid** number is restored. Without that, the number would double every generation. An answer that says *haploid* and stops has given the word; an answer that says *so the diploid number is restored at fertilisation* has given the biology.

**The membrane change is the adaptation most often missed.** It happens **after** fertilisation and its job is to stop a **second** sperm entering — because two sperm would give the wrong number of chromosomes.

steps.title: Ciliated epithelial cells
steps.body:
**Ciliated epithelial cells line the airways** — the trachea and the bronchi — and also the oviducts.

Their adaptation is the **cilia**: tiny hair-like projections on the surface that **beat in waves**.

**In the airways**, the job is done by two cells working together:

1. **Goblet cells** make **mucus**, which is sticky and **traps dust and bacteria** in the air you breathe in.
2. **Ciliated epithelial cells** then **beat their cilia to sweep the mucus** up the airway to the **throat**, where it is swallowed.

So the dirt never reaches the lungs. This is why smoking causes a cough: the smoke **damages the cilia**, the mucus is no longer swept away, and it has to be coughed up instead.

**In the oviduct**, the same beating moves the **egg** towards the uterus.

**The distinction to get right:** the **mucus traps**, the **cilia move**. A question asking what the cilia do is asking about **movement**. Saying *the cilia trap dust* describes the goblet cell's mucus and loses the mark.

steps.title: Your turn
steps.body:
**Part A.**

1. Give the difference between a eukaryotic and a prokaryotic cell.
2. Name three parts found in both an animal cell and a bacterial cell.
3. Give the function of the nucleus, the cell membrane and the mitochondria.

**Part B.**

4. Name the three parts a plant cell has that an animal cell does not, and give the function of each.
5. Name the five features of a bacterial cell given in the specification.
6. Give three adaptations of a sperm cell and say what each is for.

**Part C.**

7. Explain why both the sperm nucleus and the egg nucleus are haploid.
8. A student writes that all plant cells contain chloroplasts. Explain why this is wrong, giving an example.
9. Explain how ciliated epithelial cells and goblet cells work together to keep dust out of the lungs, and what smoking does to this.

For question 6, each adaptation needs the reason as well as the name.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**The definition of prokaryotic is the nucleus, not the size.** Prokaryotic cells are indeed much smaller, but that is an observation about them. The defining feature is that the **genetic material is not enclosed in a nucleus**. Answers that lead with size are describing rather than defining.

**Relate structure to function, because that is the spec's own wording.** Every question on 1.1 is really *why is this part shaped or placed as it is?* A muscle cell has **many mitochondria** because contracting needs a lot of energy; a sperm cell has them **packed behind the head** for the same reason. Being able to predict where mitochondria will be numerous is worth more than a list.

**Plasmids explain antibiotic resistance, and that is why they are here.** Chromosomal DNA passes to offspring. **Plasmids can pass between bacteria that are already alive**, so a resistance gene can spread sideways through a population rather than only downwards through generations. When you meet antibiotic resistance later, this is the mechanism.

**Haploid is only half an answer.** Both gametes are haploid **so that fertilisation restores the diploid number**. State the consequence. The same reasoning explains the egg's membrane change: a second sperm would make the cell **triploid**, and the embryo would not develop.

**Not all plant cells have chloroplasts.** **Root cells** do not, because there is no light underground — which is also why root hair cells are shaped for absorbing water instead. Knowing one exception shows you have understood the rule rather than memorised it.

**Keep the two airway cells apart.** **Goblet cells secrete mucus** that **traps**; **ciliated cells beat** to **move** it. Questions are set on exactly this split, and the commonest lost mark is giving the trapping job to the cilia.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Eukaryotic** cells enclose their genetic material in a **nucleus**; **prokaryotic** cells do not.
- Animal and plant cells are **eukaryotic**; **bacteria** are **prokaryotic**.
- Every cell has a **cell membrane**, **ribosomes** and **genetic material**.
- **Nucleus**: contains the DNA, which controls the cell. **Cell membrane**: controls what enters and leaves.
- **Mitochondria**: site of **aerobic respiration**, releasing energy. **Ribosomes**: site of **protein synthesis**.
- A plant cell adds a **cellulose cell wall** (strength), **chloroplasts** (photosynthesis, containing chlorophyll) and a **permanent vacuole** (cell sap, keeps the cell firm).
- **Root cells have no chloroplasts**, because there is no light underground.
- A bacterial cell has **chromosomal DNA** (a single loop), **plasmid DNA** (small rings of extra genes), a **cell membrane**, **ribosomes** and **flagella** (movement).
- **Plasmids can pass between bacteria**, which is how **antibiotic resistance** spreads.
- **Sperm**: **acrosome** with enzymes to digest through the egg membrane, **haploid nucleus**, **many mitochondria** for swimming, a **tail**.
- **Egg**: **nutrients in the cytoplasm** for the embryo, **haploid nucleus**, and the **membrane changes after fertilisation** so no more sperm enter.
- Both gametes are **haploid so that fertilisation restores the diploid number**.
- **Ciliated epithelial cells** line the airways; their **cilia beat to sweep mucus** to the throat.
- The **mucus** comes from **goblet cells** and does the **trapping**; the **cilia** do the **moving**.

questions.prompt: A bacterial cell and a human cheek cell are viewed under a microscope. Compare their structures, and explain how the differences relate to the two types of cell.
questions.solution:
The cheek cell is **eukaryotic**: its genetic material is **enclosed in a nucleus**. The bacterial cell is **prokaryotic**, so its DNA is **free in the cytoplasm** rather than in a nucleus. That single difference is what places each cell in its group, and the size difference between them follows from it rather than defining it.

Both cells share three things. Each has a **cell membrane**, which **controls what enters and leaves**. Each has **ribosomes**, which are the site of **protein synthesis** — every cell must make proteins, so no cell is without them. And each has **genetic material**, differing only in whether it is boxed in a nucleus.

The differences are in what each cell adds. The cheek cell has **mitochondria**, the site of **aerobic respiration**, which release the energy the cell needs; the bacterium has none and respires in its cytoplasm and at its membrane instead. The bacterium has its main genes on a **single loop of chromosomal DNA**, and may also carry **plasmids** — small rings of DNA holding extra genes — and **flagella**, which rotate to move it.

The plasmids are the difference that matters most. Because a plasmid can pass from one **living** bacterium to another rather than only to offspring, a gene it carries — such as **resistance to an antibiotic** — can spread **sideways** through a population far faster than breeding alone would allow. That is why the specification names plasmids, and why bacterial populations can become resistant so quickly.

questions.prompt: Explain how the structure of a sperm cell, an egg cell and a ciliated epithelial cell each fits the job that cell does.
questions.solution:
A **sperm cell** has to travel to the egg and get inside it, and every part of it serves one of those two tasks. The **tail** beats to **propel** the cell, and behind the head sit **many mitochondria**, which release by **aerobic respiration** the energy that swimming costs. At the front is the **acrosome**, a store of **enzymes** that **digest through the egg cell membrane** so the nucleus can enter.

An **egg cell** has the opposite job: to nourish what follows and to admit exactly one sperm. Its **cytoplasm is full of nutrients**, which **feed the embryo** in the days after fertilisation. Its **membrane changes immediately after fertilisation**, so that **no further sperm can enter** — a second one would leave three sets of chromosomes and the embryo would not develop.

Both gametes have a **haploid nucleus**, carrying **one set** of chromosomes. That is not incidental: it is why **fertilisation restores the diploid number** instead of doubling it each generation.

A **ciliated epithelial cell** lines the airways, and its surface carries **cilia** that **beat in waves**. Their job is **movement**: they sweep **mucus** up the airway to the throat, where it is swallowed. The mucus itself comes from **goblet cells**, and it is the mucus that **traps** the dust and bacteria. The two cells are a pair — one traps, the other clears — which is why smoking, by **damaging the cilia**, leaves mucus to build up and be coughed out instead.

examTechnique.body:
Almost every question on this topic is really the same question: **which part, and what does it do?** The specification says the structures are to be related **to their functions**, so an answer that names a part without saying what it is for has given half of what was asked. Build the habit of writing the pair — *mitochondria, the site of aerobic respiration, which releases energy* — and the marks follow.

The second habit worth building is stating the **consequence**. *Haploid* is a word; *haploid, so fertilisation restores the diploid number* is biology. The same applies to the egg cell membrane and to plasmids.
examinerErrors: Defining prokaryotic by **size** rather than by the **absence of a nucleus**.
Naming a sub-cellular structure without giving its **function**, when the question asked how structure relates to function.
Writing that **all plant cells contain chloroplasts** — **root cells** do not.
Saying that **cilia trap** dust. The **mucus** traps it; the **cilia move** the mucus.
Giving *haploid* without the reason: that fertilisation **restores the diploid number**.
Confusing **chromosomal** DNA, the single loop, with **plasmid** DNA, the small rings of extra genes.
Saying a bacterium has a nucleus, or has mitochondria. It has **neither**.
Giving the **acrosome** to the egg cell. It belongs to the **sperm**, and it is how the sperm gets in.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer **predicts** rather than recalls. Shown an unfamiliar cell packed with mitochondria, it says the cell must do energy-hungry work and gives a reason. Asked about antibiotic resistance, it reaches for **plasmids** and explains that a plasmid passes **between living bacteria**, not only to offspring, so resistance spreads sideways. Asked why gametes are haploid, it gives the consequence — the **diploid number is restored** — rather than the label. And it knows one exception to every rule it states: plant cells have chloroplasts, **except root cells**, because there is no light underground.
